Late Gvardiol strike earns Maresca winning start, Liverpool snatch last-gasp draw
item.description:
SOCCER-ENGLAND-MCI-BOU/

Manchester City's post-Pep Guardiola era began with Josko Gvardiol's stoppage-time winner earning a 2-1 victory at home to Bournemouth in Enzo Maresca's first Premier League game in charge on Sunday.

New Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola also required some even later intervention as Dominik Szoboszlai''s last-gasp penalty salvaged his side a 2-2 draw at Newcastle United, another club beginning the campaign with a new man at the helm.

An unpredictable opening weekend of the Premier League season also saw Unai Emery's Aston Villa thrashed 4-0 at Brighton and Hove Albion, all the goals arriving before halftime.

Maresca's reign began with a chastening Community Shield defeat by champions Arsenal last week and City were in danger of another loss after Marcus Tavernier slammed home a 26th-minute shot from a low ball across the area by Evanilson.

City huffed and puffed in response with newly-shaven Erling Haaland missing several chances to equalise.

But Marc Guehi, playing as a deep midfielder rather than in defence, hauled City level in the 84th minute when he rose to power home a header from a Rayan Cherki corner.

Gvardiol sparked wild celebrations with a close-range finish in the 91st minute that was initially ruled offside but allowed after a VAR overturn.

It was tough on Bournemouth and Iraola''s replacement Marco Rose as the south coast club's 18-match record unbeaten league run stretching back to January came to an end.

''The joy of the three points"

Maresca, who was welcomed with a banner unfurled in the East Stand, said it had been a perfect day despite the scare.

"I was glad when it was over also, to give them the joy of the three points. It was quite emotional and the perfect day," Guardiola's former assistant at City said.

"It's a game that we deserved to win. A game probably you don't need to win in the last eight minutes for the amount of chances we had."

Fans of Newcastle and Liverpool were united in their show of respect for Kevin Keegan at St James'' Park after the death of their shared hero, who passed away aged 75 in July.

An emotional pre-match tribute to Keegan included a huge tifo depicting the man who scored 100 goals and won seven major trophies with Liverpool and who later played for and managed Newcastle, where he was known as King Kev.

Both sets of players wore warm-up shirts bearing Keegan's name and famous No.7.

"It was probably the best fixture to happen for the first game of the season after what happened," Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot at the end of last season, said.

"It's good that both supporters can remember him like they did today."

As so often happened when the two sides met during Keegan's managerial career at Newcastle, the game had a dramatic finale as Szoboszlai robbed the home side of what would have been a great start under their new manager Matthias Jaissle.

Anthony Elanga put the hosts ahead in the fifth minute only for Cody Gakpo to level early in the second half.

Joe Willock immediately curled Newcastle back ahead having come off the bench but Lewis Hall was adjudged to have bundled over Victor Munoz and Szoboszlai lashed home the penalty in the ninth minute of stoppage time.

''Things to improve"

"I've liked a lot of the things I''ve seen from the team today," Iraola said.

"Definitely things to improve but I''ve liked the energy, especially the players coming from the bench. I think we finished the game quite strong physically."

Villa have seen their Europa League-winning side dismantled over the summer with the likes of Morgan Rogers, Lucas Digne, Youri Tielemans and Ezri Konsa all sold and the size of Emery''s rebuilding job was exposed in the south coast sunshine.

They capitulated before halftime, conceding four goals and having new signing Joao Gomes sent off.

An own goal by Victor Lindelof after eight minutes was followed by a second from Maxim De Cuyper.

Jack Hinshelwood's double inside two minutes had Brighton in dreamland and while Villa did show some character in the second half it was a worrying start to the campaign.

The Villa exodus could continue with striker Ollie Watkins left out of the squad on Sunday.

Asked why, Emery said: "Ask him. I only can answer it by silence."

The opening round of fixtures concludes on Monday with Chelsea at local rivals Fulham.

item.title: 804 complaints worth Tk 136.5 million filed on 'Ghush.site' in two days
item.description:
A new website, Ghush.site, has been launched to collect information on where and how much bribes are allegedly demanded for government services in Bangladesh.

Launched on 21 August, the platform allows people to anonymously report their experiences of being asked for bribes. In its first two days, the website received 804 reports involving a combined 136.5 million taka allegedly demanded in bribes.

The website was founded by Saif Kabeer and Shahed Sharif, two friends who said they were inspired by a similar website abroad. Their aim is to bring scattered experiences of alleged bribery onto a single platform and create an overview of which government offices and services receive the most complaints.

However, the website does not claim that the information submitted by users constitutes verified allegations or evidence.

How it works

To submit a report, users are asked to provide five pieces of information: the name of the government office, the type of service, the location, the amount allegedly demanded as a bribe and the outcome of the incident.

Users can also provide a brief description of their experience. No account is required, and the process takes less than two minutes.

The platform does not allow users to mention the name, designation or phone number of any individual.

According to the founders, the main objective is not to identify specific people but to highlight which government offices or services receive the highest number of allegations of bribery.

After a complaint is submitted, it is not published on the website immediately. They are first moderated to remove personal information. Aggressive, unclear, or policy-violating complaints are also discarded. Approved reports are then published with information on the division, office, type of service, amount allegedly demanded and the outcome.

804 reports in two days

The founders stated that 804 complaints were submitted to the site in the first two days of its launch. The total amount of money demanded as bribes in these complaints is BDT 136.5 million.

Division-wise, the highest number of complaints, 430, came from Dhaka. This was followed by 167 in Chattogram, 44 in Rajshahi, 43 in Khulna, 38 in Sylhet, 37 in Rangpur, 30 in Mymensingh, and 15 in Barishal. Eighteen per cent of the complainants stated that they had refused to pay bribes.

Reports are not proof

A key limitation of the platform is that individual submissions are not independently verified. Each published report is marked as “unverified”.

The founders state that ghush.site does not present any complaint as a true incident or as evidence against any government official or employee. It is not an investigative agency either, nor does it claim to be an alternative to the Anti-Corruption Commission. Rather, its objective is to bring people's experiences together and create an open record.

Self-funded initiative

The website is currently being run with the founders’ own funds. They said it has no formal affiliation with any NGO or organisation and has not received external funding. The website also allows voluntary donations.

Saif Kabeer, one of the founders, told Prothom Alo that they do not measure the initiative’s success simply by measuring the number of visitors.

Rather, he said, they would consider it successful if citizens could review others’ experiences before seeking government services, understand where bribes are allegedly being demanded and feel encouraged to reject unfair demands.

item.title: Bangladeshi shot dead after gunman enters New York pizza shop, another injured
item.description:
A Bangladeshi-origin man was shot dead by a gunman at a Bangladeshi-owned pizza shop in Brooklyn, New York City.

The victim was identified as Mohammad Raju, 44, from Sonaimuri upazila of Noakhali district. His wife and children live in Bangladesh.

Another Bangladeshi-origin man, 39-year-old Russell, was also injured and is undergoing treatment at a hospital.

The incident took place at around 11:30 pm last Saturday at American Best Wings and Pizza on Rockaway Avenue in Precinct 73.

After receiving the report, a team from the New York City Police Department arrived at the scene at 12:01am and rescued the two gunshot victims. They were taken to Brooklyn Health-Brookdale University Hospital Medical Centre.

Raju, who had been shot in the chest, was pronounced dead by physicians on duty after being taken to the hospital. No one involved in the incident has been arrested yet. Police are investigating the incident.

Mohammad Russell, Raju’s colleague who is undergoing treatment at the hospital, told the media, “A Black man entered the shop and shot me directly without saying anything. I fell to the ground after being shot in the thigh. Later, the man also shot Raju, who was working as a cashier. He was shot in the chest. The pizza shop is owned by a friend of Raju. Raju looked after the shop as if it were his own.”

Shop owner Abdul Jalil said, “Raju was my friend. He would look after my shop as if it were his own. His home was in Kongshonagar village of Amishapara Union in Sonaimuri upazila of Noakhali. Raju’s wife and two young children live in Bangladesh.”

Jalil said, “Raju came to the United States three years ago. He has no relatives here. Financial assistance from the Bangladeshi community is needed to send his body back to Bangladesh. We hope Bangladesh Society and other associations will extend active support.”

Bangladeshi immigrants in the United States have demanded a proper investigation into the incident and urged authorities to quickly bring the gunman involved to justice.

item.title: Human trafficking in the digital age: Emerging challenges and the way forward
item.description:
Participants

Ali Akbar Khan, Additional Inspector General (in charge), Criminal Investigation Department (CID), Bangladesh Police;

Rebeka Khan, Joint Secretary (Political-1 Wing), Ministry of Home Affairs;

Tanvir Hassan Zoha, Prosecutor and Special Investigation Officer, International Crimes Tribunal;

Dr BM Moinul Hossain, Professor and Director, Institute of Information Technology, University of Dhaka;

Salma Ali, Chairperson, Action Against Trafficking and Sexual Exploitation of Children and Women (ATSEC) South Asia, and Adviser, Bangladesh National Women Lawyers’ Association;

Nurul Quader, Programme Manager (Migration), Human Resources Development Sector, Delegation of the European Union to Bangladesh;

Dipta Rakshit, Project Director, Ashshash, and Country Representative, Winrock International Bangladesh;

Tasneem Binte Karim, National Programme Coordinator, UNODC, South Asia;

Shakirul Islam, Chairperson, Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Programme (OKUP);

Mahmudul Hasan, Legal Officer, Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU);

Md Al Amin Noyon, President, Anirban Survivors’ Voice;

Monnan Chhoyal, Bangladeshi returnee from a scam centre in Cambodia;

Naznin Akter, Bangladeshi returnee from Malaysia;

Key note speaker:

Shariful Islam Hasan, Associate Director, Migration Programme and Youth Platform, BRAC

Moderator: Firoz Choudhury, Assistant Editor, Daily Prothom Alo.

Ali Akbar Khan

Additional Inspector General (in charge), Criminal Investigation Department (CID), Bangladesh Police

One of the biggest challenges in investigating human trafficking is collecting information and evidence across borders and tracing technology-enabled financial transactions. Investigating cryptocurrency, hundi and online transactions requiresadvance technology, specialised training and international cooperation. At the same time, it is essential to enhance investigators’ technological skills and establish effective mechanisms for international information sharing. Cooperation from various international organisations is playing an important role in strengthening capacity in this region.

Cyber scam centres in Cambodia, the risky route to Italy through Libya and luring people through social media are all part of transnational criminal networks. Many people travel on tourist visas and subsequently fall victim to scams, while some victims are later drawn into trafficking others. As the driving forces behind these crimes are often based outside the country, the problem cannot be solved through measures taken within Bangladesh alone.

Many people were subjected abuse abroad reach settlements after returning home or are unwilling to testify. This undermines the pursuit of justice. Therefore, diplomatic missions, law enforcement agencies, international organisations and all relevant ministries must work together through  coordinated efforts, alongside investigative agencies.

I believe technology-enabled human trafficking can be brought under control to a significant extent by strengthening regular migration, conducting effective campaigns against irregular migration, increasing technology-based surveillance, enhancing international information exchange and taking coordinated initiatives to counter traffickers’ misinformation and propaganda on social media. Long-term planning, regular assessment and monitoring, and trust-based cooperation among the relevant agencies will be essential to achieving effective results.

Rebeka Khan

Joint Secretary (Political-1 Wing), Ministry of Home Affairs

The dynamics of human trafficking is changing rapidly, while the use of technology has made this crime more complex. Coordinated efforts by the government, international organisations and all relevant stakeholders are therefore essential. The new law enacted in 2026 has included migrant smuggling and scams through fake online job advertisements alongside human trafficking. The biggest challenges now are effective implementation of the law and preventing fraud in regular migration processes.

Many Bangladeshis who migrate abroad for work face risks of fraud, abuse, exploitation and often forced into criminal activities. To address this situation, the government is working to implement a national referral mechanism and formulate the National Plan of Action (NPA) 2026–30 so that victims can receive coordinated protection, legal assistance and necessary services. At the same time, information sharing among agencies involved in migration, telecommunications and expatriate welfare is being strengthened. The use of modern technologies, including Passenger Name Record and the Advance Passenger Information System at airports, is being expanded to detect fraudulent travel documents, strengthen investigative capacity, improve inter-agency coordination and ensure rapid information exchange. Bilateral and regional cooperation to combat cyber scam centres in Cambodia and other countries has also been strengthened.

Legal action is being taken swiftly against people involved in human trafficking, including government officials. Sharing experiences, exchanging information, mutual cooperation, capacity building and coordinated initiatives will further strengthen our ability to combat technology-enabled crime. This will help achieve effective and sustainable progress in preventing technology-enabled human trafficking.

Tanvir Hassan Zoha

Prosecutor and Special Investigation Officer, International Crimes Tribunal

Field-level experience shows that in many cases, people are lured  abroad, subjected to abuse and then held for ransom. However, victims can be brought back and traffickers arrested if swift and coordinated action is taken. Therefore, frontline police must be given greater authority, necessary support and the ability to make quick decisions in combating human trafficking.

Such crimes cannot be addressed by central agencies alone. Police at the station level, sub-inspectors and constables collect much of the information at the local level. Their skills, technological capacity and investigative expertise must be strengthened. Modern surveillance systems, data analysis and a national human trafficking intelligence platform are needed to combat technology-enabled crime.

My experience in international training shows that coordinated policies, rapid information sharing and effective investigation are more important than technology alone. The law enforcement agencies abroad have the capacity to take immediate action based on complaints received.

In Bangladesh too, law enforcement agencies must be given greater scope to make quick decisions, take effective action and use modern technology. At the same time, the necessary infrastructure and skilled personnel must be ensured for technology-based investigations.

I believe we must move away from the practice of repeatedly using the police for political interests and ensure an environment where they can work professionally.  It will not be possible to effectively combat human trafficking, cyber fraud and other forms of organized crime without addressing the practical challenges at the field level, making effective use of advanced technology, ensuring adequate manpower and providing necessary authority to law enforcement agencies.

BM Moinul Hossain

Professor and Director, Institute of Information Technology, University of Dhaka

The involvement of middlemen in human trafficking continues and the use of technology has increased at an alarming rate. Traffickers are operating in increasingly organised ways through fake job advertisements, AI-generated videos, cryptocurrency, technologies that conceal identities and covert messaging apps. Even mainstream media outlets are sometimes misled when trying to identify AI-generated videos. As a result, it has become even more difficult for ordinary people to identify scams. The misuse of technology has made human trafficking a more complex form of transnational crime. Traditional awareness-raising activities alone cannot address this crisis. Targeted campaigns must be conducted in areas from which people are more vulnerable to trafficking. At the same time, social media data analysis, the use of open-source information and technology-based surveillance must be strengthened.

Law enforcement agencies must develop modern technology-based skills beyond conventional investigation methods. Otherwise, it will not be possible to effectively confront technologically sophisticated  criminal networks. International digital platforms, including Meta, must be brought under greater accountability. This cannot be achieved through administrative decisions alone; it requires sustained diplomatic initiatives and international cooperation. At the same time, existing state information and surveillance systems must be used more effectively. Timely action can lead to significant progress in preventing technology-enabled human trafficking.

Salma Ali

Chairperson, Action Against Trafficking and Sexual Exploitation of Children and Women (ATSEC) South Asia, and Adviser, Bangladesh National Women Lawyers’ Association

There has been considerable progress in legislation, policy, victim protection and the justice process. Provisions for victim protection and several aspects of investigation and prosecution have improved. CID and other agencies have also received training to combat unsafe migration and human trafficking. Yet unsafe migration and human trafficking continue. Cross-border cooperation, skilled investigation and speedy justice remain major challenges in cases of technology-enabled trafficking. Trials in many cases take a long time, while many victims ultimately do not want to pursue cases because of concerns about privacy. As a result, organised criminals often escape justice.

The Ministry of Home Affairs has taken many initiatives, but human trafficking in the name of migration continues through land ports, airports and sea routes.

From my field experience, I have seen that suspicious passengers can be identified through just a few minutes of observation at an airport. Recently, a young woman travelling to Nepal was identified as suspicious, and efforts were made to rescue and bring her back to Bangladesh. This shows that many trafficking incidents can be prevented if there is commitment and effective surveillance. However, gaps in coordination and accountability among border points, airports and relevant agencies remain.

In my view, the most urgent priorities are effective coordination among ministries, an uncompromising stance and accountability. At the same time, investigators, government prosecutors and judges must be -trained; police must receive regular training and supervision; and organised traffickers must be brought to justice swiftly. Only then will visible change be possible and victims be protected from repeated abuse.

Nurul Quader

Programme Manager (Migration), Human Resources Development Sector, Delegation of the European Union to Bangladesh

Human trafficking, particularly the rapidly expanding trafficking linked to scam centres and technology-enabled exploitation linked to scam centres, is a serious violation of human rights. Addressing such crimes requires a comprehensive, victim-centred approach combining prevention, protection, prosecution and strong partnerships. It is essential to address the root causes of vulnerability, expand safe and regular migration pathways, strengthen cross-border cooperation and enhance digital investigation capacity. At the same time, alongside ensuring justice for survivors, effective support must be provided for their sustainable rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

The European Union welcomes Bangladesh’s recent progress in legislation and policy. It also reaffirms its commitment to supporting the effective implementation of these initiatives through programmes on safe migration, rehabilitation, prevention of human trafficking and migrant smuggling, migration management, skills development and integrated border management.

We believe that the government, international partners, law enforcement agencies, the justice system, civil society and all relevant stakeholders must work together to address complex and transnational crimes such as human trafficking. Alongside strengthening preventive measures, the rights, protection, justice and dignity of survivorsmust be given the highest priority. Mutual trust, information sharing, effective coordination and long-term cooperation will be the most important foundations for achieving this goal.

Dipta Rakshit

Project Director, Ashshash and Country RepresentativeWinrock International Bangladesh

No one knowingly consents to become a victim of human trafficking. People take risks in the hope of getting better jobs, a safer life and opportunities to improve their circumstances not to become victims of trafficking. After working on this issue for 20 years, I feel I have failed. Although the Bangladesh government has enacted laws and formulated national plans and policies to prevent human trafficking, there are still major gaps in implementation. Information from people returning from Cambodia shows that 80 percent of them went abroad through regular migration processes. We must therefore find the answer to how such fraud is taking place.

Human trafficking has now become a technology-enabled crime. The crisis therefore cannot be addressed by raising awareness through traditional methods alone.

Counter-campaigns must be conducted on the same social media platforms where people are being lured by false promises. Courtyard meetings, programmes in schools and colleges or drawing competitions are no longer enough. At the same time, effective monitoring and accountability must be ensured for financial transaction channels, including bKash, Nagad, hundi and cryptocurrency. The flow of money generated through human trafficking must also be brought under strict monitoring.

There is no alternative to coordinated action to prevent human trafficking. People must be made aware through real-lifeexamples, safe migration opportunities must be expanded for vulnerable groups, and social media platforms must also be held accountable. Effective coordination among all relevant organisations must be ensured. Only then can meaningful progress be made in combating technology-enabled human trafficking.

Shariful Islam Hasan

Associate Director, Migration Programme and Youth Platform, BRAC

Irregular migration is damaging Bangladesh’s image. Bangladeshis are now among the largest groups attempting to reach Europe by crossing the Mediterranean from Libya. Many suffer severe abuse in Libya, while many others lose their lives at sea. At the same time, many Bangladeshis and Rohingya are attempting to reach Malaysia by crossing the Bay of Bengal. Reports say nearly 500 Rohingya have died over the past week. Many people in Malaysia are also being lured into scams with promises of migration opportunities  to Australia.

Social media has now become a major tool for traffickers. The operations and tactics of human trafficking are becoming increasingly complex and technology-driven. Our research shows that 82 percent of young people in Bangladesh would like to leave the country if given the opportunity. In their desperation to go abroad, many faces various risks. Many falls victim to cyber scams. In June alone, 583 people returned to Bangladesh from Cambodia after falling victim to cyber scams, while the number has reached 1,800 so far in 2026. Of them, 98 percent did not receive the jobs they had been promised, 88 percent were held captive, 87 percent had forged documents, 66 percent had travelled through brokers, 38 percent suffered severe psychological trauma and 27 percent were physically abused.

The government has enacted new laws and formulated a national plan of action to combat human trafficking and migrant smuggling. But proper implementation of the law remains the biggest challenge. It is essential to raise awareness, strengthen legal protection against cyber scams, bring criminal networks to justice, create employment opportunities at home, facilitate regular migration and enhance regional cooperation to prevent trafficking. Bangladesh cannot address such transnational crimes alone.

Tasneem Binte Karim

National Programme Coordinator, UNODC, South Asia

Human trafficking linked to scam centres is a relatively new crisis for Bangladesh. Although these issue has been addressed in South-East Asian countries for sometime now, however the past one to two years, people from Bangladesh and other South Asian countries are increasingly falling victim to it. There is a lack of reliable national data, research and evidence-based analysis on the issue. Evidence-based information is essential for effective policymaking, prevention and accurate assessment of the situation—including how many Bangladeshis are being trafficked through fraudulent recruitment, how many are returning home, how many are receiving rehabilitation and justice, and how prepared the relevant agencies are to combat the crime.

In my experience, compared to many other South Asian countries, Bangladesh’s law enforcement agencies have relatively strong technological capacity. The capabilities of specialised agencies, particularly CID, must be used more effectively. However, conventional investigation methods alone are not sufficient to combat technology-enabled human trafficking. Alongside developing modern technology-based investigative capacity in areas such as cryptocurrency, social media and open-source intelligence, regular training for law enforcement agencies must be ensured.

The new law is an important step forward. Its effective implementation is now the biggest challenge. Building the capacity of judges, government prosecutors and investigators, strengthening regional and bilateral cooperation, and expanding awareness both at the field level and through social media are essential. At the same time, the government, development partners and civil society must work together to provide information on regular migration pathways and warn people about technology-enabled scams.

Shakirul Islam

Chairperson, Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Programme (OKUP)

Although the discussion began with technology, I would primarily like to highlight the lack of coordination within the state. When it is said at the highest level of the state that many migrants knowingly take risky routes, that reflects the government’s perspective. Yet we keep talking about making migrants aware while failing to take effective action against local brokers and those involved in trafficking networks. This is the state’s biggest failure. At a recent exchange meeting in Madaripur, the district administration also said that it knew the traffickers but did not have the authority to take action against them. Bringing them under the law would have sent a strong message to society.

In 2019, we provided support in case filed by a woman who had returned from a middle eastern country after experiencing abuse. A lengthy investigation found elements of human trafficking, but in 2025, a judge at the special tribunal proposed an out-of-court settlement. The survivor clearly said she wanted justice and dignity, not money. Yet the case was ultimately settled for slightly more than Tk 400,000. Such an outcome is deeply disappointing in a serious crime like human trafficking.

I believe the root problems are the lack of political will and effective coordination. Workers are going abroad after obtaining clearance from the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET), so the state must also take responsibility for that process. It is not enough to talk about coordination at meetings and seminars; coordinated action by all state institutions must be ensured in practice.

Mahmudul Hasan

Legal Officer, Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU)

A new law has been enacted to prevent human trafficking, incorporating issues related to migration and the illegal trafficking of people. But I believe the justice system is still not receiving adequate attention. It can take two to three years for human trafficking related lawsuits to move from investigation to trial. During this time, many survivors are unable to continue pursuing their cases. After spending lakhs of taka to go abroad and becoming financially devastated, they often cannot afford to pursue a lawsuit for years. Many also lose a day’s income when they have to attend court.

Human trafficking tribunals were established to ensure speedy justice, but there are still major weaknesses in case investigations. There is no dedicated or specialised investigative agency for the tribunals. As a result, investigation reports are not submitted on time, and in many cases, investigations are not conducted properly. This means that the key facts of the cases do not come to light and allows the criminals to escape justice.

The most important question for me is whether we are able to ensure justice. If justice is ensured, it will create fear among criminals. Another major concern is that there has been no judge at the Dhaka Human Trafficking Tribunal for five months. The absence of a judge at such a sensitive tribunal is depriving justice seekers of timely justice.

Md Al Amin Noyon

President, Anirban Survivors’ Voice

After working on human trafficking for many years, I have come to believe that diplomatic failure is also a factor behind the problem. There is a lack of coordination between ministries. Over the past one and a half years, 56,000 Bangladeshis have gone to 28 countries through BMET where Bangladesh has no embassy or consulate. We do not even know how they are doing or whether they are safe.

During the same period, 16,000 workers went to Cambodia. While working with them, we found that many were taken there with employment visas but were later given tourist visas and sold into scam networks. Yet they had travelled following government procedures.

BMET is also responsible for monitoring whether workers reach their workplaces and whether their salaries and accommodation are in order. If the state wants, it can identify how many people travelled on tourist visas and did not return and bring those responsible to account. This would reduce the risk of human trafficking.

At the same time, people returning from scam centres must be treated not as criminals but as survivors. Regular monitoring, rehabilitation and mental health services must be ensured so that they do not end up becoming involved in criminal networks again.

Monnan Chhoyal

Bangladeshi returnee from a scam centre in Cambodia

I went to Saudi Arabia in 2022. After staying there for three years, I returned home and decided to go abroad again. A relative from my area sent me to Cambodia for Tk 500,000, saying that I would get a job at a restaurant. After completing training, I went to Cambodia on 5 December 2025. A few days later, I was taken to a Chinese company. When I arrived, I saw thousands of people working on computers.

I was instructed to use the name “Maria” and build relationships with people on Instagram to scam them and collect money. I told them I had not been informed about such work. But they had my passport. I was told that if I did not want to work, I would have to paythe money to get back my passport, which was impossible. I was later forced to work.

When I failed to meet the assigned targets, I was beaten and locked in a small room. I was eventually rescued during a police raid. As I did not have my passport, returning home became difficult. With BRAC’s assistance, I was provided with a travel pass and a ticket and returned to Bangladesh.

Later, the accused party filed a counter-case against me in retaliation for the human trafficking case. Now I am an accused myself, and I do not have the money to fight the legal battle. .

Naznin Akter

Bangladeshi returnee from Malaysia

I was struggling to support my two children because of financial difficulties. I had divorced my husband five years ago. To get out of debt, I decided to go to Malaysia for work. Through an acquaintance, I was offered a restaurant job with a monthly salary of around Tk 60,000. However, I had to pay more than Tk 250,000 to go there. I sold jewelry and borrowed money to arrange the amount. I told them I would pay the remaining Tk 5,000 after joining the job, and they agreed.

On 15 November 2025, I was taken to Malaysia on a visit visa. I had also been taught in advance what to say at immigration. After arriving, my passport, ticket and documents were taken away. I was told that I would not be given any job unless I paid the remaining money.

I was also pressured to collect money from my family. Later, I was kept at a hotel and then taken to a locked room, where I was held for six consecutive days. I was assaulted simply for asking where I was. Finally, with the efforts of my brothers, I was able to return to Bangladesh on 21 November.

Recommendations

  1. Develop specialised institutional capacity to ensure swift investigation and trial of human trafficking cases.

  2. Strengthen the capacity and training of law enforcement agencies to detect technology-enabled crimes.

  3. Enhance coordination among BMET, law enforcement agencies, diplomatic missions and relevant ministries.

  4. Strengthen information sharing and international cooperation to combat transnational human trafficking.

  5. Ensure strict and effective monitoring of cryptocurrency, hundi and online financial transactions.

item.title: Salman Shah murder: CID seeks 7-day remand of Don
item.description:
The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) has sought seven days' remand for Ashraful Haque Don, who is currently in jail in connection with the murder case of actor Salman Shah, citing three reasons.
Inspector Mojibur Rahman of the CID's Dhaka Metro South, the investigation officer in the case, submitted the remand petition last Thursday.
On Monday, Shah Alam of the prosecution department said Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Jewel Rana has fixed Thursday for the hearing in the presence of the accused.
First , the case is highly sensitive and has generated widespread public interest as the victim was popular film actor Salman Shah. His mother, Neela Chowdhury, has been demanding an impartial investigation since his death in 1996. The CID believes interrogating Don in custody could help uncover the truth behind the case.
Second , the investigation officer described Don as a “cunning” person and said intensive interrogation in police custody could help identify the whereabouts of other people allegedly involved in the case and facilitate their arrest.
Third , the CID wants to question Don about why and under whose influence he allegedly attempted to flee abroad despite a travel ban, saying this could help reveal information about the case.
Don was arrested by immigration police at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on August 9 and subsequently handed over to the CID. He was sent to jail the same day. His bail petition, filed on August 12, was rejected by the court.
On October 20 last year, Salman Shah's brother, Mohammad Alamgir Kumkum, filed the case on behalf of their mother, Neela Chowdhury.
On September 6, 1996, film actor Salman Shah, whose real name was Chowdhury Mohammad Shahriar Emon, died at his flat in Eskaton, Dhaka. He was at the peak of his popularity in the Bangladeshi film industry at the time.
Following his son's death, Salman's father, Kamaruddin Ahmed Chowdhury, initially filed a case of wrongful death. However, on July 24, 1997, he sought to have it converted into a murder case, alleging that his son had been killed.
The court subsequently directed the CID to investigate the murder allegation alongside the wrongful-death case. On November 3, 1997, the CID submitted a final report stating that Salman Shah had died by suicide.
Rejecting the report, Kamaruddin filed a revision petition. On May 19, 2003, the court ordered a judicial inquiry.
After 11 years, Metropolitan Magistrate Imdadul Haque submitted the inquiry report on August 3, 2014, which also dismissed the murder allegation.
After Kamaruddin's death, Neela Chowdhury continued pursuing the case. On February 10, 2015, she objected to the judicial inquiry report and named 11 people whom she alleged could have been involved in her son's death.
The case was subsequently investigated by the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB). However, following a state objection, Judge Imrul Kayesh of Dhaka Special Judge Court-6 ordered RAB to stop investigating the case on August 21, 2016.
The Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) then took over the investigation and submitted its final report on February 25, 2020, after four years of investigation.
The PBI said it had analysed the statements of 54 witnesses and examined seized evidence but found no evidence supporting the murder allegation.
According to the PBI report, Salman Shah was suffering from family disputes linked to his relationship with actress Shabnur and mental distress over distancing himself from his mother, Nilufa Chowdhury alias Neela Chowdhury, due to his relationship with his wife, Samira Haque. The report concluded that he had died by suicide.
Neela Chowdhury rejected the report and sought further investigation into her son's death.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Mamunur Rashid accepted the PBI report and ordered the accused to be discharged on October 31, 2021.
Salman's family subsequently filed a revision petition before the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court, raising several objections.
On June 12, 2022, the Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court admitted the revision petition, but the hearing was delayed for various reasons.
On October 20, the 6th Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge of Dhaka, Md Jannatul Ferdous Ibn Haque, allowed the revision petition filed by Salman Shah's mother concerning his death. The court ordered the filing of a murder case, attaching Kamaruddin's complaint and the statement of Rizvi Ahmed alias Farhad, who was allegedly involved in the incident, and directed Ramna Model Police Station to investigate and submit a report.
In the case, Mohammad Alamgir alleged that the accused named in the complaint, along with unidentified absconding suspects, had planned and conspired to kill Salman Shah on September 6, 1996.

item.title: ICC confirm sanctions for Jaiswal and Fernando
item.description:
India batter Yashasvi Jaiswal and Sri Lanka bowler Asitha Fernando have been sanctioned by the ICC following their incident on the opening day of the second ICC World Test Championship fixture in Colombo.
Both players were found to have breached Article 2.12 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which relates to “inappropriate physical contact with a Player, Player Support Personnel, Umpire, Match Referee or any other person (including a spectator during an International Match).”
As a result, Jaiswal and Fernando were fined 25 per cent of their match fee and were handed one demerit point each.
Both players didn't have any previous offences in the preceding 24-month period.
The incident occurred in the 17th over of India's batting innings after Fernando dismissed Jaiswal. The India batter walked towards Fernando and the two exchanged words, after which Fernando moved his head towards Jaiswal. In response, Jaiswal leant in, resulting in their heads making contact.
Both players admitted the offences and accepted the sanctions proposed by Andy Pycroft of the Emirates ICC Elite Panel of Match Referees, so there was no need for formal hearings.
India and Sri Lanka have been locked in an intense battle in the second Test in Colombo.
Rain brought play to a halt in the second session on day 2, with India reaching 475/8 and Dhruv Jurel unbeaten on 95, just five runs away from his second Test century.

item.title: Prime Minister's Delhi visit: Conditions, strategy or opportunity?
item.description:
The relationship between India and Bangladesh is not merely political; it is based on deep economic and strategic interdependence. Golam Rasul writes about the considerations that should be taken into account regarding the decision for the Bangladeshi Prime Minister's visit to Delhi.

The potential visit of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to India is becoming an important test of Bangladesh's foreign policy. Shortly after assuming office in February, India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi invited him for a bilateral visit. At the same time, Bangladesh has also been invited to participate in the expanded session of the 18th BRICS Summit, scheduled to take place in New Delhi on 12-13 September, this time as the current chair of BIMSTEC. Thus, the political and diplomatic significance of the two upcoming invitations is not the same: the first is part of bilateral relations, while the second is related to Bangladesh's broader regional responsibilities.

In this context, the issue of Sheikh Hasina's extradition has become intertwined with the India visit. Dhaka has stated that a favourable environment is needed for the Prime Minister's visit to India, and has simultaneously called on New Delhi to expedite the extradition requests of Sheikh Hasina and other fugitives.

India has stated that it has received Bangladesh's request and the matter is under consideration in their legal process. Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman has also tried repeatedly to clarify the difference between the two types of invitations. However, in public discourse, the bilateral visit, extradition, and regional responsibilities of BIMSTEC often become conflated.

Here arises the main diplomatic question: Will the demand for Sheikh Hasina's extradition be a precondition for the Prime Minister's visit to India, or will the visit itself be used as a diplomatic tool to achieve this demand? The question is not merely about making the visit or not; rather, it is about which course of action can most effectively advance Bangladesh's national interests.

What Bangladesh First means

The phrase "Bangladesh First" is not merely an analytical framework. It is a slogan frequently uttered by BNP Chairperson Tarique Rahman himself, and the party has highlighted it as a guiding principle of their declared foreign policy. Thus, whatever stance the government ultimately takes regarding the visit to India and the extradition issue will be a test not only of diplomatic wisdom but also of the coherence of the government's own declared policy.

To give real meaning to this slogan in foreign policy, it means neither blind allegiance to any country nor blind opposition. It means evaluating every decision based on Bangladesh's sovereignty, security, economic interests, and long-term strategic interests. The same principle applies in the context of relations with India. Therefore, Sheikh Hasina's extradition, the Prime Minister's bilateral visit to India, and Bangladesh's participation in the expanded BRICS session as the chair of BIMSTEC must be viewed not as isolated incidents but in the context of Bangladesh's larger national interests.

Extradition: The demand remains firm, but not a precondition

There is an extradition treaty between Bangladesh and India from 2013. Bangladesh has formally requested Sheikh Hasina's extradition; India has acknowledged receiving the request and stated that the matter is under review within their legal framework. There is no reason for Bangladesh to back down from this demand; it involves questions of judicial accountability, the rule of law, and respect for Bangladesh's own judicial processes.

However, maintaining a legitimate demand and turning it into a precondition for every aspect of bilateral relations are two different things. Bangladesh has the right to stand firm on the issue of extradition; at the same time, determining which diplomatic approach would be most effective in securing that demand is also part of statecraft. This is where the difference lies between an emotion-driven position and strategic statecraft.

If the Prime Minister's visit to India is seen as a concession to New Delhi, then a fundamental reality of diplomacy is overlooked. High-level visits themselves are a tool for negotiation. Through such visits, state leaders convey political messages, prioritise their interests, negotiate demands, and try to define the framework for future relationships.

There are important examples of this in international diplomacy. During Nixon's visit to China in 1972, the Taiwan question was not resolved; rather, the path for dialogue and normalisation of relations was opened while differences remained. In South Asia, despite the unresolved Kashmir dispute in 1999 during Vajpayee's Lahore visit, the Lahore Declaration created a framework for dialogue and confidence-building measures. Although the subsequent Kargil conflict disrupted this process, it proved the necessity for dialogue and the resolution of disputes as separate matters.

The general lesson from these experiences is that not resolving a dispute and not holding discussions on the dispute are not the same things. Often, high-level political communication is most needed amid unresolved disputes, as the purpose of diplomacy is not always to achieve immediate solutions, but rather to break deadlocks, create negotiation opportunities, and place one's interests at the centre of discussions.

Thus, issues should be linked but not tied to a singular demand. Hasina's extradition is an important issue for Bangladesh, so it cannot be removed from the bilateral agenda. However, it would not be diplomatic wisdom to hold long-term issues like water, trade, energy, connectivity, and border management hostage to this one demand. In other words, extradition will be on the table for discussion, but not everything in the relationship will depend on it.

India should be clearly communicated that progress in extradition is essential for political trust, but parallel progress on other issues is also expected. In this approach, Bangladesh can maintain both principled firmness and flexibility in negotiation; because diplomatic influence depends not only on what is being demanded but also when and in what context the issue is brought forward.

Bangladesh's larger interests: Water, trade, and regional leadership

The relationship between India and Bangladesh is not just political; it stands on deep economic and strategic interdependence. Water is its clearest example. The Ganges Water Treaty of 1996 is set to expire next December; bilateral discussions on its renewal have already begun before its expiration. The distribution of water from common rivers, including the Teesta, remains an unresolved issue for a long time.

Trade relations are deep but imbalanced—though the merchandise trade between the two countries is nearly $11. 4 billion in the fiscal year 2024-25, Bangladesh's exports amounted to approximately $1.76 billion while imports were around $9. 62 billion. Mutual interests are also involved in energy, electricity, and connectivity. Therefore, Bangladesh's diplomatic goal should not be limited to whether ‘India will return Hasina’—the bigger question is how this mutual dependency can be directed towards a more reciprocal and balanced relationship.

The broader calculation is also connected with the added responsibility of the BIMSTEC chair. Confusing the invitation to the expanded BRICS session with the bilateral visit would be a mistake. This invitation is not for Tarique Rahman personally but rather for Bangladesh as the current chair of BIMSTEC, an organisation headquartered in Dhaka. Here, Bangladesh is representing a regional alliance of seven nations, not merely acting as a bilateral party.

Absence from this session would not only increase distance from India but also result in losing the opportunity for direct discussions with BRICS leaders and weaken Bangladesh's leadership position as the chair of BIMSTEC. It would inadvertently send a wrong message to Nepal, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Bhutan, and Thailand, suggesting that Bangladesh is uninterested in fulfilling its regional leadership responsibility. Hence, merging bilateral visits and BIMSTEC-BRICS participation into the same negotiating package is illogical; it is crucial to view them in separate diplomatic contexts—one for bilateral relations and the other for regional leadership.

Strategic firmness: Turning the visit into a diplomatic tool

Hasina's extradition is a highly sensitive issue in the Bangladeshi public mind; thus, the government should stand firm on it. However, firmness and rigidity are not the same. Firmness means not compromising on core interests, while rigidity means adopting a stance that could limit one's path to achieving those interests. A policy of ‘no visit unless extradition happens’ might restrict important diplomatic channels. Conversely, maintaining the demand for extradition while utilising the visit as an opportunity for broader bilateral discussions will be strategically more effective. Here, the visit itself becomes a diplomatic tool, not a concession.

If the visit eventually occurs, it should not be a mere courtesy call. Bangladesh should approach it with a clear diplomatic package at the centre of which should be—Sheikh Hasina’s extradition; fair renewal of the Ganges Water Treaty; water management of common rivers including Teesta; cessation of border killings and border management; additional market access for Bangladesh’s exports and the abolition of land-port-based trade restrictions imposed in 2025; real initiatives to reduce the trade deficit; cooperation in energy and electricity and mutual economic benefits in connectivity. In other words, instead of getting the relationship stuck on a single issue, using that issue to renegotiate the entire relationship afresh—this is the practical application of the ‘Bangladesh first’ policy. The visit should be turned into an effective diplomatic tool.

Final words

There is no reason for Bangladesh to back down from the demand for Sheikh Hasina’s extradition. However, turning this demand into such a stringent precondition that it narrows the opportunity for high-level direct negotiations is not diplomatic wisdom. Bangladesh’s policy should be neither blind loyalty to India nor unnecessary opposition. Similarly, adopting a stance merely to show firmness that shrinks one's negotiating space would also not be right.

"Bangladesh First" means that the ultimate measure of every decision will be the national interest. While extradition is important for that interest, water, trade, energy, borders, connectivity, and regional leadership are equally vital. Therefore, Bangladesh's policy should be: firmness in demands, pragmatism in negotiations, and national interest in outcomes.

If participating in the Prime Minister's visit to India and the expanded session of BRICS as the BIMSTEC chair can be effective diplomatic tools to achieve those interests, then that opportunity should not be missed. The demand should remain firm but keep the doors of diplomacy open because success is not only evaluated by what we demand but ultimately by what Bangladesh achieves from those demands.

item.title: TOP SHOTS (24 August 2023)
How extracurriculars can fast-track your corporate career
item.description:
It was 2019. I was nurturing a dream of building a career at a good corporate organisation after my graduation. But the path was quite an unknown area. I did not know where or how to begin.

Although I had been somewhat involved in extracurricular activities since my college days, I fully immersed myself in such activities upon stepping into university. In my first year, I got the opportunity to work as an organiser for a major international event.

At every event, I had opportunities to meet and interact with new corporate professionals and introduce myself in new ways. Alongside organising international programmes such as Hult Prize and APUF, I also achieved success in quite a few business case competitions.

Then I realised just how valuable those university experiences had been in 2022. While still in my final year, I began my professional career at 10 Minute School, one of the country’s largest edtech platforms. After working there for two years as a call centre team leader, I got the opportunity to join the business development team at Prothom Alo, the country’s leading newspaper.

Working here has given me the opportunity to collaborate directly with vice-chancellors of some of the country’s renowned universities, CEOs of major corporate organisations and brand heads.

At this stage of my career, I can clearly see that if I had not been involved in extracurricular activities during my university years, adapting to the corporate world would not have been nearly as easy.

For those who are just beginning their university journey or preparing to enter professional life, my advice is:

• Overcoming hesitation is the first step

In today’s digital age, it is difficult to keep pace by relying solely on CGPA. Alongside academic studies, students should participate in extracurricular activities and case competitions to overcome mental barriers and fear.

• Stepping out of your comfort zone

This is particularly important for those who want to build a career in marketing or sales. You must step outside your comfort zone. The more challenges you put yourself through, the faster you can grow in your career.

• Networking and communication

The professional networks built through event management or club activities can open the door to enormous opportunities in working life.

Employers today do not look only at academic results. They also assess your problem-solving abilities and leadership qualities. So start preparing yourself right from your campus days.

After all, opportunities are always waiting for a prepared mind.

Education officials had earlier indicated that the examinations could begin in mid-March. The decision has now been finalised.

item.title: Nahid Islam: Government has completely failed in 180 days
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) convener and opposition chief whip Nahid Islam has said the government is reverting to the old authoritarian style of governance, alleging that BNP leader Tarique Rahman has no real plan for running the country.
Nahid made the remarks at an emergency press conference held at the party's makeshift central office in Bangla Motor, in the capital, on Monday afternoon.
The press conference was organized by the NCP's Policy and Research Sub-Committee to highlight what the party described as the "failures" of the BNP-led government's first 180 days in office.
He said the past 180 days of the government have painted a picture of mismanagement, adding that the administration is steering the country toward ruin "in a fascistic manner" through widespread plunder and partisan appointments across state institutions.
He warned that the divisional long march under the 11-party alliance would deliver a stern message to the government.
At the event, the NCP released a booklet titled "From the Promise of Change Back to Old Politics: Mismanagement, Inefficiency, Lack of Planning."
The booklet states that at its first cabinet meeting on February 17, immediately after assuming power, the government had set three priorities for its first 180 days: keeping commodity prices under control, improving the law-and-order situation, and ensuring a steady supply of electricity and energy.
Six months on, the NCP argues that data and ground realities show the government has failed dismally on all three fronts. Factories are shutting down amid the energy crisis and workers are losing their jobs, the booklet claims, while farmers are being forced to buy fertiliser at inflated prices.
The unprecedented crisis in fuel oil, gas and electricity has severely disrupted industrial production, agriculture and everyday life, the booklet says, pointing to rising prices of essential goods.
It further alleges that banking-sector defaulters are making a comeback, old syndicates have become active again in the consumer-goods and import markets, and that BNP has emerged as a new partner within these syndicates.
The NCP contends that five months of inactivity at the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) and the resurgence of loan defaulters and market syndicates are linked.
On the institutional front, the booklet alleges that reforms left behind by the interim government, including the Human Rights Commission, the anti-enforced-disappearance law, and the Supreme Court Secretariat, have been dismantled one by one and replaced with weaker, less effective legislation.
It also claims that the widely publicised 31-point charter and the party's own election manifesto have been discarded, giving way to blatant partisan appointments and nepotism within state institutions.
The document further states that there has been no visible progress in the trials over the July mass killings, and that justice for victims, along with treatment and rehabilitation for martyrs' families and the injured, is absent from the government's stated priorities.
According to the booklet, attacks and legal cases filed by ruling-party activists against opposition figures and journalists have continued to rise, with even administration officials facing harassment.
In most such cases, it alleges, victims of attacks rather than the attackers are the ones facing legal harassment, while the police force is once again being turned into a partisan force.
The NCP also accused the government of violating its electoral pledges and the July Charter by failing to have the Constitution Reform Council take its oath. Overall, the booklet concludes, the BNP government's 180 days have become emblematic of inefficiency, mismanagement, lack of foresight, and dishonesty.
Speaking at the press conference, Nahid Islam said the energy sector has been devastated over the government's 180 days in power.
Despite pledges to dismantle syndicates, he alleged, the government has instead strengthened partisan syndicates of its own.
He claimed the government promised to disband the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) but is now reportedly planning to retain it under a different name.
He further alleged that partisan administrators have been installed in city corporations and district councils, and that a form of disorder now prevails across sectors, including a deteriorating law-and-order situation, though he said the opposition continues, from its position, to point out the government's mistakes.
"We are continuously showing the people where the government is going wrong and where it is breaking its promises, and we are doing this at the policy level," Nahid said. "We will show this to the people, and we will politically resist it if the government continues down this path."
He said the booklet released to mark the government's 180 days was deliberately titled to reflect how the administration is reverting to the same fascistic, authoritarian structure it once claimed to be dismantling. "These 180 days have proven that Tarique Rahman has no plan whatsoever to run the country," Nahid said. "He has simply taken power and is running the country according to the same old fascist policies and plans. He is driving the country toward destruction."
He added that the 11-party alliance had, at a meeting the previous day, announced plans for a long march across five to six divisions, to be followed by a mass rally in Dhaka. "Through that rally, we will deliver a strong message to the government. If further movement is needed after that, we will announce it," he said.
Nahid Islam said the government had been given six months to work, yet Bangladesh's Constitution has still not been amended or reformed, and the plan to further empower the opposition under the July Charter has not been implemented. As a result, he said, the opposition remains weak in parliament and is often not given the opportunity to speak.
He said that if the government feels it lacks an adequate plan, it should seek policy support from the opposition, noting that his party has offered such support on various occasions in the past.
"We can say that BNP functioned as a failed opposition party in Bangladesh for the last 16 years," he said.
Responding to a question, Nahid alleged that instead of dismantling old syndicates, new partnerships have formed in their place, that institutions are being subjected to partisan appointments, and that regulatory bodies are being weakened through inadequate legislation.
He said the democratic and political environment is shrinking, with rising attacks and harassment against opposition figures, journalists and administrative officials, with little to no action taken against the perpetrators in most cases.
He added that the aspirations of the July uprising, including justice for the mass killings and treatment for the injured, remain absent from the government's list of priorities. He said his party had wanted an accountable state structure, but oversight bodies such as the ACC, the Human Rights Commission and the Ombudsman remain ineffective, and that multiple points of the widely publicised one-point election demand have been abandoned within these six months, with the government itself violating its own commitments.
"In these 180 days, we believe the government has completely failed," Nahid said, attributing the failure to a lack of planning, corruption and mismanagement. He pointed to the recent cabinet reshuffle as evidence, noting that a government which once claimed to have a clear plan is now seeking policy suggestions from the opposition, while ministers and state ministers are being reshuffled. "At this rate, at some point there may even be a need to change the prime minister," he said.
He anticipated that BNP would argue six months was sufficient time to judge the government's performance. "But the interim government wasn't even given three months," he said. "And even if six months isn't an entirely fair yardstick, they shouldn't be claiming success the way they are. They should be apologising for the gas and electricity crisis that people across the country are suffering through, for the factories shutting down. They promised economic management and reform of the administration and law and order, but they have failed to deliver on any of it. After another six months, this government will no longer be able to blame the interim government or the Awami League government for its failures; that excuse will no longer be acceptable to the public."
Also present at the press conference were NCP political council member Saleh Uddin Sifat, joint convener Advocate Tariqul Islam, and other senior party leaders.

item.title: Humaiun: New phase in Bangladesh’s foreign policy to boost global visibility
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Monday said Bangladesh’s foreign policy has entered a new phase, with the government now focusing on strengthening bilateral and multilateral relations and raising the country’s global visibility and influence.
Speaking to reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on his first working day as the State Minister, Kobir said the new responsibility is a continuation of the work he was doing as the Prime Minister’s Adviser on Foreign Affairs.
“It is not the first day of work as such. Work is about continuity,” he said, adding that the new assignment requires the government to “hit the ball… ground running.”
He said a strategic framework for Bangladesh’s foreign policy has been established over the past six months and that the government would now begin rolling out engagements based on that foundation.
“Over the last six months, we have established a strategic framework for our foreign policy. It has a strong, solid foundation now,” Kobir said.
“From that, now we will roll out our engagements. And we will… build our relations, bilateral relations, multilateral relations from a position of strength.”
He said the government would now focus on putting substantive content into Bangladesh’s bilateral relationships and hoped to take the country’s “visibility, influence… to great new heights.”
Kobir said he is already familiar with senior officials at the Foreign Ministry, having worked with them over the past six months.
“The assignment is new, but it is an assignment that is an extension of further work in the sphere that I have already been working in,” he said.
Expressing confidence in the Ministry and its officials, he said,”Together… we can take Bangladesh, Insha’Allah, into a new horizon.”
He said Bangladesh should be recognised as a country with strong soft, medium and other forms of power and influence.
‘I am Bangladeshi’
Asked about reports and social media discussions concerning his British citizenship and whether he had renounced it before assuming the state ministerial position, Kobir responded sharply. “I am Bangladeshi,” he said.
“Here, Bangladesh… Bangladeshi… I don’t think there is anybody that will question my Bangladeshism and my stand.”
Responding to questions about social media reports, he added, “I come with citizenship, and you talk about netizens! I mean, which netizens?”
Kobir also referred to the political period involving Moeen U Ahmed and Fakhruddin Ahmed, asking whether “the heartburn of Moeen U Ahmed, and Fakhruddin” was “acting up again.”
He urged media, citizens and political leaders to unite in the national interest.
“All people who take a strong stance for the country, patriotic people who are here, those who stand by the country—all of us including the media, the citizens, the political leaders, we will all unite and take this country forward, Insha’Allah,” he said.
He then urged reporters to focus on substantive issues related to his ministry.
Asked about the Mecca Defense Pact, Kobir said Bangladesh expressed interest in it but indicated that there has been no new development.
“No, no, we have expressed interest,” he said.
He said Bangladesh’s growing international recognition is creating greater interest among key stakeholders in the Middle East and the wider Muslim world.

He added that key stakeholders are inviting Bangladesh’s leadership, particularly Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, to participate in discussions and enengagements.

item.title: Nusrat’s mother satisfied with HC verdict, seeks security for family
item.description:
Shirin Akter, mother of madrasah student Nusrat Jahan Rafi, on Monday expressed satisfaction over the High Court verdict in the widely discussed murder case of her daughter and sought security for her family, alleging that they have received threats.
“I am satisfied with the verdict, Alhamdulillah,” she told reporters at her home in the Char Chandia area of Sonagazi upazila in Feni following the verdict.
Shirin said some people had tried to portray Nusrat's death as a suicide after the incident. “But today's verdict has once again proved that it was a murder,” she said.
She alleged that they were threatened with arson attacks on their home and harm to family members, seeking security for her family from the authorities concerned, including Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
Sub-Inspector Palash Chandra Roy of Feni Model Police Station, who is part of the security detail, said additional security measures were taken around the family's home to prevent any untoward incident following the verdict.
The High Court on Monday upheld the death sentences of two convicts in the Nusrat murder case after hearing death references, appeals and jail appeals filed in the case.
The two convicts are Siraj-ud-Daula, expelled principal of Sonagazi Islamia Senior Fazil Madrasah, and Shahadat Hossain alias Shamim.
The court also commuted the death sentences of four convicts to life imprisonment and acquitted 10 others.
The lifers are Nur Uddin, Saifur Rahman Mohammad Jobayer, Jabed Hossain alias Sakhawat Hossain and Umme Sultana alias Popy.
Those got acquitted are Maqsood Alam alias Moksud, a former councillor and former general secretary of Sonagazi municipality Awami League; Hafez Abdul Quader; Absar Uddin; Kamrun Nahar Moni; Abdur Rahim Sharif; Iftekhar Uddin Rana; Imran Hossain alias Mamun; Ruhul Amin, president of Sonagazi Upazila Awami League and former vice-president of the madrasa; Mohiuddin Shakil; and Mohammad Shamim.
According to the prosecution, Siraj-ud-Daula sexually harassed Nusrat in his office on March 27, 2019. He was arrested after a case was filed over the incident.
On April 6, 2019, Nusrat was taken to the roof of the madrasah building after she refused to withdraw the case against the principal. Her hands and legs were tied, and kerosene was poured over her before she was set on fire.
Nusrat died on April 10 while undergoing treatment in a Dhaka hospital.
Her elder brother Mahmudul Hasan Noman filed a case with Sonagazi Police Station over the incident, which was later turned into a murder case.
On October 24, 2019, Feni Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal Judge Mamunur Rashid sentenced all 16 accused, including the suspended principal Siraj Ud Doula, to death.

item.title: PM for reviving girls’ stipends to curb dropout, child marriage
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday directed the authorities concerned to examine the feasibility of reintroducing universal stipends for girls from Class VI to the degree level, aiming to encourage them to continue their education and help prevent child marriage.
He gave the directive at a meeting on the Prime Minister’s Education Assistance Trust at the Prime Minister’s Office in the Cabinet Division of the Secretariat.
The meeting was informed in detail about the trust’s ongoing activities, its goals and role in preventing students from dropping out by providing financial assistance during their education, said Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
The impact and achievements of the universal stipend programme for girls, introduced during the tenure of former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia, were also discussed.
The programme was credited with helping increase girls’ school attendance, encouraging them to continue their studies and discouraging child marriage.
Against this backdrop, the Prime Minister asked the authorities to assess the possibility of reviving universal stipends for girls from Class VI to the graduation level.
He stressed the need for preparing a clear proposal after analysing the possible cost, number of beneficiaries, implementation process and expected social and educational impact of the programme.
The meeting also discussed providing stipends to boys on the basis of merit and eligibility to encourage them to pursue education.
Besides financial support, the meeting put equal emphasis on students’ nutrition and health as important factors for improving the quality of education.
Various aspects of the school-level mid-day meal programme, including its management, nutritional value and ways to ensure safe preparation and supply of food for children, were discussed.
The Prime Minister stressed that food provided to students must be nutritious, safe and of good quality, and said there should be no compromise over food standards.
The meeting also discussed two alternative approaches to implementing the mid-day meal programme, taking into account cost, management efficiency, local participation and quality control.
Tarique Rahman directed the authorities to launch pilot projects in two separate districts, with each district testing one of the proposed approaches, to assess their effectiveness, feasibility and potential outcomes.
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon, Prime Minister’s Education Affairs Adviser Mahdi Amin, Secondary and Higher Education Division Secretary Abdul Khaleque, PM’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon and other relevant officials attended the meeting.

item.title: Bangla QR transactions cross Tk110cr
item.description:
Following the mandate of Bangla QR under Bangladesh's 'One Nation, One QR' policy, the volume and total value of transactions have increased significantly.
While daily transactions averaged around Tk37 crore at the beginning of July, the figure surged past Tk110 crore last week.
According to Bangladesh Bank data, replacing proprietary QR codes of various institutions with the unified Bangla QR was made mandatory starting July 1 this year.
Since then, transaction growth on the platform has accelerated rapidly.
In early July, an average of 178,000 Bangla QR transactions occurred daily, accounting for purchases worth approximately Tk37.33 crore.
Last week, the average daily transaction volume rose to nearly 303,000, with the daily financial value reaching roughly Tk110.38 crore.
In effect, since the launch of the unified QR system, the daily number of Bangla QR transactions has nearly doubled, while the total transaction value has roughly tripled.
Meanwhile, on July 1—the day the unified QR policy took effect—the number of Bangla QR merchants nationwide stood at around 1.6 million.
That figure has now expanded to nearly 3 million.
Along with private commercial banks, state-owned banks are playing a lead role in expanding Bangla QR adoption.
Industry stakeholders believe that implementing a unified QR system across all banks and mobile financial services (MFS) will simplify digital payments and drive the country's transition toward a cashless economy.

item.title: ICT-2 sends 3 journalists to jail in crimes against humanity case
item.description:
The International Crimes Tribunal-2 on Monday ordered three senior journalists to be shown arrested and sent to jail in crimes against humanity case related to the July uprising in 2024.
The three journalists are former Bhorer Kagoj editor Shyamal Dutta, Ekattor TV managing director and editor-in-chief Mozammel Babu, and its chief correspondent Farzana Rupa.
Earlier, the tribunal had ordered the jail authorities to produce the three before it on Monday.
Prosecutor Faruk Ahmed represented the prosecution during the hearing, while prosecutors Zahirul Amin, Marjina Raihan, Tarek Abdullah and others were present.
Faruk Ahmed told the tribunal that production warrants were issued against the three journalists on August 17 in connection with the crimes against humanity case relating to the July uprising.
As they were produced before the tribunal on Monday, the prosecution sought to show them arrested in the case and send them to jail.
